Chennai businessman donates 121 kg of gold ornaments to Tirumala temple
articles.summary: A Chennai-based couple, Vardhaman Jain and Radhika Jain, donated gold ornaments weighing 121 kg worth Rs 207.6 crore to Lord Venkateswara at the Tirumala temple on Thursday, November 26, in the presence of Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu. According to Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams (TTD), Vardhaman Jain, co-founder and vice-chairman of Chennai-based healthcare business process outsourcing (BPO) company Access Healthcare, accompanied by his wife Radhika, his brother and company co-founder Anurag Jain, and other family members offered the ornaments, embedded with diamonds and other precious stones. They were handed over to the temple authorities inside the hill shrine and the donation is considered the largest single-day individual offering of ornaments in the temple's recorded history. Before the handover, Chief Minister Chandrababu Naidu, accompanied by his wife Nara Bhuvaneswari, offered prayers at the temple. The ornaments were first displayed at the Ranganayakula Mandapam, where Naidu, the donor family and officials viewed the collection. The family members along with Naidu later participated in the ceremonial procession of the ornaments, carrying it on plates over their heads, from the Ranganayakula Mandapam to the Ananda Nilayam, the temple's sanctum. TTD Specified Authority Chairman and Executive Officer Muddada Ravichandra, Additional Executive Officer Ch Venkaiah Chowdary, temple priests and senior officials received the offering and honoured the donor family with traditional silk shawls and sacred prasadam. Of the total 121 kg of gold, 106 kg was used to craft ornaments for Lord Venkateswara, while the remaining 15 kg of pure gold would be used to make a golden saree for Goddess Padmavati Ammavaru at Tiruchanoor. The ornaments include a diamond-studded golden crown, a tiger-claw pendant, ear ornaments and necklaces, waist belt, and protective covers for deity's feet and anklets. According to the TTD, the ornaments contain 2,916.5 carats of precious stones, including 2,247.7 carats of blue sapphires, 91.6 carats of yellow sapphires, 84.2 carats of rubies and emeralds, and 238.2 carats of diamonds. Their estimated value is Rs 207.6 crore, including making charges. Speaking to the media, Vardhaman Jain said the decision to donate 121 kg of gold was rooted in his family's gratitude towards the deity. "I don't know why I originally committed to donating 121 kilos of gold. It later turned out to be the exact weight of gold that the Lord wears every single day," he said. Jain said he had initially approached TTD officials with the intention of donating 121 kg of raw gold after selling a majority stake in Access Healthcare to New York-based private equity firm New Mountain Capital in January 2025, with the deal reportedly worth over Rs 6,000 crore. However, following a meeting with Naidu, the donor was persuaded to have the gold converted into specially designed ornaments instead of handing it over in its raw form that the process took approximately 15 months. Jain said that the meeting scheduled for five minutes eventually lasted an hour, during which the Chief Minister and temple authorities discussed the proposed offering. "The Chief Minister was most curious as to how I came up with that specific number, and we realised it was purely a divine number," Jain said and also thanked the Chief Minister's Office for monitoring the progress of the offering and following up on it every week. The family had initially preferred to keep the donation anonymous, but Naidu encouraged them to come forward, saying their contribution could inspire others. Meanwhile, addressing the media, CM Naidu described witnessing the 121 kg gold offering as a “historic moment.” The Chief Minister also recalled surviving the Alipiri bomb attack, saying that he believed the deity's blessings had saved his life. "Lord Venkateswara gave me a new lease of life. It was his blessings that saved me," he said. Naidu had also announced plans to construct 5,000 temples across Andhra Pradesh with TTD's support and establish Lord Venkateswara temples with annaprasadam facilities in all state capitals and major Hindu diaspora centres abroad. Emphasising the importance of service to society, Naidu said the principle of 'Manava Seve Madhava Seva' (service to humanity is service to God) should guide devotees and appealed to wealthy individuals to follow the Jain family's example and use their wealth for social welfare, spiritual causes and the benefit of underprivileged communities. He had also assured devotees that contributions made to TTD would be utilised transparently for the welfare of pilgrims.

articles.summary: Ade Kailash, a 42-year-old man from Telangana, was arrested for allegedly killing his daughter Kalyani two days before her engagement, after she refused to marry the man he chose for her. On November 25, Umri panchayat secretary Rajanna Bhamani went to the village and learned about Kalyani’s death from other residents. He was told that Kailash performed Kalyani’s funeral rites in a rush, and that he cremated her body on a funeral pyre before 9 am on November 24 without waiting for their relatives to arrive. In his complaint to the police, Rajanna said that as per the customs of their tribal community, unmarried girls were not cremated on a funeral pyre. He further learned that Kalyani’s marriage was arranged and her engagement was scheduled to take place within the next two days. This raised Rajanna’s suspicion, and he lodged a complaint with the police. Police have booked Kailash for murder and causing the disappearance of evidence.

articles.summary: The Madras High Court on Friday, November 27, permitted bye-elections to the Ambasamudram and Perundurai Assembly constituencies. However, it ruled that polls to Tiruchi (East), Viralimalai and Karur cannot be held until the court decides on the election petitions pending against the results in those constituencies. The bench of Chief Justice Sushrut Arvind Dharmadhikari and Justice G Arul Murugan passed the order after hearing a petition by Tirunelveli-based advocate K Venkatachalapathy. Through his counsel, Venkatachalapathy had sought to defer bye-elections to all five constituencies until the election petitions were decided. The petitioner had filed the plea to declare that the vacancies did not constitute “clear vacancies” or available vacancies for the purpose of holding bye-elections under Section 151-A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The vacancy in Tiruchi (East) arose after Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay, who won from both Tiruchi (East) and Perambur, resigned from the former and retained the Perambur seat. In Viralimalai, Karur, Ambasamudram and Perundurai, AIADMK MLAs C Vijayabaskar, MR Vijayabhaskar, Esakki Subaya and S Jayakumar, respectively, resigned from the Assembly and joined the ruling Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK). According to LiveLaw, the petitioner told the court that several winning candidates had resigned after the Assembly election and that the Speaker had accepted their resignations, even as election petitions challenging their victories were pending. The State, however, argued that a vacancy arises once the Speaker accepts a resignation. The Advocate General said that, in at least three cases, no election petition was pending when the resignations were accepted, and that petitions filed later could not retrospectively invalidate vacancies. The respondents also questioned the petitioner’s standing, arguing that he was not a registered voter in any of the constituencies.

articles.title: Heavy rains lash Thiruvananthapuram, Thampanoor among worst affected areas
articles.summary: Heavy rains lashed Thiruvananthapuram, Keralam’s capital city, on Thursday, November 26. Waterlogging brought traffic and normal life to a temporary standstill on major roads in the two hours when the rains were heaviest. The episode triggered criticism from political leaders and residents over alleged lapses by the Thiruvananthapuram City Corporation, ruled by the Bharatiya Janata Party, including pre-monsoon cleaning. Thampanoor was among the worst-affected areas, with knee-deep water submerging roads leading to the Central Railway Station and the KSRTC bus terminal. The Meteorological Department had issued a yellow alert for nine districts, including Thiruvananthapuram, on Thursday, warning of thunderstorms, lightning and winds in isolated places. East Fort recorded 91 mm of rainfall in just 90 minutes. Several parked cars and two-wheelers were partially submerged, while water entered shops and commercial establishments. Commuters heading to the railway station and bus stand were forced to wade through muddy water, with traffic movement severely disrupted. The police diverted light vehicles from flooded stretches, and the water reportedly took around two hours to recede after the rain stopped. The situation was reportedly aggravated by garbage and plastic waste spilling onto roads from the Amayizhanchan canal, further obstructing the drainage network. The flooding once again raised questions about the city's preparedness and drain maintenance. District collector Anju KS said unusually intense rainfall and high tide around noon had hindered the smooth discharge of rainwater. Mayor VV Rajesh said a drain had been closed during ongoing work near Attakulangara and that officials had been directed to investigate the blockage, the Times of India reported. Opposition leaders alleged that inadequate pre-monsoon cleaning and clogged drains contributed to the flooding. Former minister V Sivankutty and former mayor V K Prasanth staged a protest at the Thampanoor police station, accusing the civic body of failing to respond to the situation on the ground. LDF leaders also questioned the corporation's claims of having completed pre-monsoon cleaning, alleging that funds allocated for the work had been spent without adequate monitoring. Mayor V V Rajesh, who was in Goa on an official visit, said unusually heavy rainfall had caused unexpected blockages and that the matter would be examined. Following the protests, the district administration said a review meeting would be held. The Mayor also called a Health Circle meeting on Friday to assess the waterlogging and discuss remedial measures.

articles.summary: Kerala Chief Minister VD Satheesan on Thursday claimed that his phone is being tapped and that he sometimes deliberately gives incorrect information on calls to mislead those listening in. He was speaking at a Constitution Day programme organised by the Dr BR Ambedkar Chair at the University of Kerala on Thursday, November 26. "Everyone is under the surveillance of the state. When we speak, when we get into a car, when we enter our house, when we enter a room, in all these moments, we are under someone's watch," he said. Satheesan, who does not handle the home portfolio, however did not specify which agency was carrying out the alleged monitoring. He said he no longer feels anxious about it, as he accepts he has "no secrets" and is always being watched. Recalling his college days, Satheesan said George Orwell's 1984, which portrays citizens under constant state watch, left him tense and insecure for a month. In a post on X later, he described the Constitution as "far more than a legal document", calling it the "soul of our nation" and "a promise of dignity, liberty, equality and justice to every Indian". He noted that Ambedkar, a consistent critic of Mahatma Gandhi and Jawaharlal Nehru, was still chosen by Nehru as Law Minister in his first Cabinet. This, he said, reflected the spirit of inclusiveness in the Constitution. "Today, as technology increasingly influences what we think, preserving our capacity for independent thought remains one of our greatest challenges," he wrote. He added that the greatest tribute to the Constitution's architects would be to safeguard an India that protects every individual's dignity and rights "without dividing people in the name of religion, caste or language".

DMK awaits delimitation bill draft, wary of BJP’s assurances on 50% seat increase
articles.summary: Amid speculation that the DMK could back the BJP-led Union government’s proposed delimitation bill, The News Minute has learnt that the party is still weighing its position, with concerns over whether its demands will be incorporated into the legislation. The DMK has not seen the draft bill and says it will not commit to supporting it until it has examined the provisions. While the BJP has agreed in principle to one of the party's key demands, the DMK is not convinced that the government can provide a legally binding guarantee on the other. The DMK has two conditions for supporting the proposed exercise: a 25-year freeze on delimitation and a uniform 50% increase in the number of Lok Sabha seats across all states, without altering their relative share of representation. According to DMK sources, while the BJP has agreed in principle to the extension of the freeze, there are concerns about whether the 50% increase can be written into the bill. The proposed legislation is understood to be a precursor to setting up a Delimitation Commission, and prescribing the formula for the exercise before the commission begins its work could undermine its autonomy, sources said. This is the dilemma holding the DMK back. An oral assurance from the government on the floor of Parliament that every state will receive a 50% increase in seats would not be legally binding. The party wants a guarantee in the legislation itself, rather than one that could ultimately be left to the discretion of a future commission. It also wants to examine whether any other changes have been made to the draft that could have implications for Tamil Nadu and through that, the DMK. An MP from the party told TNM that the party has not seen the draft bill and cannot take a position without examining it. “We have not seen the draft bill and cannot agree to anything until we do,” she said. Reiterating the party's two conditions, the MP said the 25-year freeze must continue and there must be a 50% increase in seats across states. However, she said the DMK would have to examine whether any other changes had been made to the new draft that could affect its position. “We still cannot say yes to the bill unless we see the draft, in case something else has been altered,” she said. Another DMK MP told TNM that nothing about the contents of the proposed legislation had come to his knowledge. He said the party could not take a decision before seeing the draft. A source familiar with the DMK's position told TNM that whatever decision the party takes will be in the interest of Tamil Nadu. The source also said that if the proposed legislation fails to pass, the state could face Census-based delimitation, which would not be beneficial to Tamil Nadu. BJP appears more confident of numbers this time The DMK's hesitation comes at a time when the BJP appears to have made progress in securing the numbers needed to push the legislation through Parliament. After its defeat in the Lok Sabha in April, the BJP seems to have worked on building support ahead of bringing the bill back. Sources familiar with the BJP's calculations say the defections of Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) and Trinamool Congress (TMC) MPs have improved its position. The party is also banking on support from some regional parties and the possibility of parties such as the Samajwadi Party abstaining, which could lower the number of votes required for the Constitution Amendment Bill to pass. The BJP is seeking a two-thirds majority for the legislation. What happened in April The Union government had first attempted to push through a package of legislation linking delimitation with the implementation of 33% reservation for women in the Lok Sabha and state Assemblies during a special sitting of Parliament in April. The government introduced the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026, seeking to facilitate an increase in the strength of the Lok Sabha and state Assemblies. The proposed framework also included a separate Delimitation Bill and legislation relating to Union Territories with legislatures. The Constitution Amendment Bill was defeated in the Lok Sabha on April 17, failing to secure the two-thirds majority required for its passage. A total of 298 MPs voted in favour and 230 against it. The government subsequently did not proceed with the other two linked bills. The DMK had opposed the proposed framework, arguing that a delimitation exercise based on population could disadvantage southern states that had successfully implemented population-control measures. The party had sought two safeguards: an extension of the existing freeze on delimitation for another 25 years and a uniform 50% increase in the number of seats across states. During the debate, Kanimozhi had questioned Union Home Minister Amit Shah's assurance that southern states would not lose their relative representation. She had asked what would happen if the Delimitation Commission did not follow the Home Minister's assurance. The DMK's argument was that such a guarantee had to be part of the law and could not rest on assurances made in Parliament. Parliament to reconvene from November 30 The latest developments come after Union Parliamentary Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju announced on November 26 that the government had requested the Lok Sabha Speaker and Rajya Sabha Chairman to reconvene the two Houses for essential government business. The Lok Sabha is scheduled to meet on November 30, while the Rajya Sabha will reconvene on December 2. The sittings could conclude on December 3, depending on the business before the Houses. Although the government has not officially announced the legislative agenda, the proposed sitting has triggered speculation that it will bring back the delimitation legislation and the linked women's reservation framework. For the DMK, the immediate decision will depend on what the revised draft actually provides. While the party is open to considering an increase in the number of parliamentary seats, it wants to ensure that Tamil Nadu's share of representation is protected through a provision that a future Delimitation Commission cannot override. Until it sees that protection in writing, the party is not prepared to commit its support.

articles.title: A Duck’s Tale: Arun Varghese on his quirky satire rooted in the backwaters of Kuttanad
articles.summary: Ducks, wobbling about on land and water, are such a common sight in small towns of Kerala, especially in Kuttanad, that you don’t pause to take a second look when you hear their ceaseless quacking. So, when A Duck’s Tale , a Malayalam movie set to premiere at the International Film Festival of Kerala (IFFK) next month, begins with a flock of ducks swimming in the night, you don’t think much of it, beyond making a vague connection to the title. But Arun Varghese, who grew up in Kuttanad, manages to pick out a single duck from that flock and weave several stories around it, in his debut film. He has written and directed A Duck’s Tale with the production team that made the critically acclaimed Baakki Vannavar , released two years ago. Salmaanul, who played the quiet protagonist in Baakki Vannavar , turns into an expressive, frustrated young man in A Duck’s Tale , with both films putting him in the garb of an unemployed youth. “Yes, but in this case it is more because he is lazy, not trying hard, while Baakki Vannavar was more about the system,” Arun says in an interview with TNM. Malayalam film Baaki Vannavar explores unemployment through a gig worker's life He too, like the protagonist, is an engineering graduate, and had a stint in the IT sector for a few years before reconnecting with a passion that began in childhood, making films. “It was all short films before, which I mostly wrote for and sometimes directed. It had continued in my IT days in Bengaluru too,” Arun says. Arun Varghese In his first feature film, Arun chooses a few incidents from his childhood, connects them to the ducks he was so used to seeing in his hometown, and looks at serious issues through a lens of humour. Children play a big part in the film, with the whole story set off by a little boy who is upset because he is not offered duck curry at a friend’s home. “That is from my childhood, a story I don’t remember but had heard about. I was the child who was upset at not getting the duck curry,” he says. For the film, he picked children from schools in Kuttanad. They speak the language, know the terrain, and move comfortably across the fields and along the backwaters. One of the child actors in 'A Duck's Tale' Salmaanul shows his range, playing a man going through multiple troubles, including unemployment and relationship issues. He is nothing like the sad gig worker in Baakki Vannavar . Pramod Velliyanad is another versatile actor, playing the overly meddlesome local leader, who is everywhere and wants to stick his nose into everything. Women characters, the mothers and the lover, are thoughtfully written, distinct, and adorably genuine, especially the sister in the family that Pramod visits. The music, by Neeraj Remesh, is also a welcome addition, noticeable as it stretches in a sequence of two boys cycling down a road, talking about their evening game, before one of them continues to walk into a shocking situation. You might spot, if you look for it, a few drawbacks or areas to improve. But it is an admirable debut, original in its theme and treatment, lacking any pretentiousness in becoming an offbeat satire. A Duck’s Tale has been chosen in the Malayalam Cinema category of the IFFK, which begins on December 11.

articles.title: Filmmaker Sraiyanti on Auto Queens and the ‘amount of power women feel when together’
articles.summary: Propped up on a boat resting on the shore, looking out at the evening sea, Leela and Mohana eat their meals and joke about fish. “I have older fish because I am older and you have young fish because you are younger,” Leela, adorable and funny as she is with Mohana, says, laughing. Two auto-rickshaw drivers relaxing at the end of a working day is how Auto Queens , a documentary on the camaraderie and struggles of a group of women workers in Chennai, begins. The film, made by cinematographer-director Sraiyanti, was screened at the International Documentary and Short Film Festival of Kerala on September 26. “The idea came to me from a friend, Mathivannan, who is one of the producers. Their company was doing some work with Veera Pengal Munnetra Sangam (VPMS), the women-led auto rickshaw and transport workers union in Chennai,” Sraiyanti says. The VPMS began as a Whatsapp group in 2018 to address the many issues faced by women rickshaw drivers, including a lack of parking space. It was later registered in 2024. Mohana and Leela, who lead the organisation, are also thick friends, having serious conversations about the issues faced by women drivers at one moment and pulling each other’s legs at another. Sraiyanti manages to capture a beautiful balance between the two parallel stories, with the free and uninhibited conversations of women, when they come together, becoming both endearing and inspiring. Still from 'Auto Queens' Scenes of the union’s gathering in a room are full of surprising candour and humour. Their simple and straightforward answers to problems at work and home are so wonderfully articulate that after watching it, you might just want to run to your own group of women friends, close the door, and simply unwind. “The amount of power the women feel when they are together, you can sense it in the room. There is no holding back – how women are when we are together versus when we have to have walls up for the outside world, you can see those walls breaking inside the union office,” Sraiyanti says. She has not given them a script or asked them to do anything specific, she simply put them in favourable situations, like the beach where Mohana and Leela converse. Quite by chance, though, she manages to shoot an argument that the short-tempered Leela has with a male driver who asks her to move her vehicle. Mohana later tells her to show some patience, even as she, too, asserts that no woman needs to hold back when she is treated unfairly. Adding to the emotion that comes from the women’s easy camaraderie is the music – old Tamil songs like ‘Aayirathil Oruthi Amma’ and ‘Paadatha paatellam’ – that flows into the screen with such perfect timing. It is lovely to see the women enjoy their time, listening to their favourite songs and singing along, even as Mohana jokes that Leela’s partner left her because of her singing. The film, at less than half an hour, seems to end all too soon, and Sraiyanti has been told by many women that they wanted to continue watching this story. The women in the VPMS union who appear in the film watched it together at a screening and were quite emotional about how it turned out, Sraiyanti says. Their fight continues, and membership has more than doubled in the years since. Sraiyanti approaches the film both as a gender rights issue as well as a portrayal of community support. “We cannot not address the gender issue but the bigger thing for me through the film was to show how, having such community support, having people backing you, gives you strength as an individual struggling to make a living.” Sraiyanti, too, has worked her way up to directing her first documentary independently. She has been a cinematographer for the past 10 years. She began with documentaries, shooting films with Premkrishna Akkattu, who shot Auto Queens . Later, they became cinematographers on feature films such as Sai Pallavi’s Gargi and the Malayalam film Detective Ujjwalan . However, she says, her interest has always been in non-fiction films. Before Auto Queens , Sraiyanti and Prem made a short film called Tambaram Cooking , which also premiered at the IDSFFK a few years ago.
